summary.simple: Our home galaxy. The Sun, Earth and most of the stars you can see at night are inside it. Because we live inside it, nobody has ever photographed the whole Milky Way from outside.

facts.text: The Milky Way is about 100,000 light-years across.
Our solar system is about 26,000 light-years from the centre of the Milky Way.
Our Sun, with Earth, takes about 250 million years to travel once around the centre of the Milky Way.

image.alt: Artist's illustration of the Milky Way seen from above: a glowing yellow bar across the centre, with blue spiral arms of stars winding out from its ends.
image.illustrationNote: Artist's concept, not a photograph. We live inside the Milky Way, so no camera has ever been outside it to take a picture of the whole galaxy. This drawing shows what scientists think it looks like from above.

summary.simple: A small, irregular galaxy that travels around our Milky Way. From the Southern Hemisphere it looks like a faint, glowing patch in the night sky.

facts.text: The Large and Small Magellanic Clouds orbit each other as well as our Milky Way.
The Large Magellanic Cloud is about one-tenth the size of the Milky Way, with only 1 percent of its mass.
The Magellanic Clouds are named after Ferdinand Magellan, who led an expedition to sail around the world in 1519.

facts.text: The Small Magellanic Cloud is only half the size of the Large Magellanic Cloud.
It may once have been a barred disk, pulled out of shape by the gravity of the Milky Way and the Large Magellanic Cloud.

summary.simple: The nearest big galaxy to our own. On a dark night you can see it without a telescope, as a faint smudge of light.

facts.text: In our sky, the Andromeda Galaxy looks six times as wide as the full Moon.
Hubble's 2025 picture of Andromeda shows the glow of 200 million stars, and that is still only part of the galaxy.
The first known written report of the Andromeda Galaxy is in a book from the year 964 by the Persian astronomer al-Sufi.

summary.simple: A spiral galaxy about half the size of our Milky Way. It is the third-largest galaxy in our Local Group, after Andromeda and the Milky Way.

facts.text: On average, new stars are forming in the Triangulum Galaxy ten times faster than in the Andromeda Galaxy.
In the 1920s, Edwin Hubble studied stars that change in brightness in this galaxy, and proved it is a separate galaxy outside our own.
Under very clear, dark skies, keen-eyed people can just see it without a telescope.

facts.text: M81 is one of the brightest galaxies in the night sky.
Through binoculars, M81 and its neighbour M82 can be seen together in the same view.
A black hole with the mass of 70 million Suns sits at the centre of M81.

summary.simple: A galaxy where new stars are being born extremely fast, stirred up by the pull of its neighbour, M81.

facts.text: Around its centre, young stars are being born 10 times faster than in our whole Milky Way.
This burst of star formation will probably die down in a few tens of millions of years.
The Cigar Galaxy shines brightly in infrared light.

summary.simple: A giant spiral galaxy that faces us, so we look straight down on its arms, like looking at a pinwheel.

facts.text: The Pinwheel Galaxy is about 170,000 light-years across, nearly twice as wide as our Milky Way.
Astronomers estimate that it contains at least one trillion stars.
Pierre Méchain, one of Charles Messier's colleagues, discovered it in 1781.

facts.text: It has nearly 2,000 globular star clusters, about 10 times as many as our Milky Way.
Its mass is equal to about 800 billion Suns.
A massive black hole is thought to sit in its bright centre.

The Whirlpool's spiral arms are star-making factories: they squeeze hydrogen gas and create clusters of new stars.
Charles Messier discovered it in 1773.

facts.text: M87 is home to several trillion stars, a supermassive black hole and about 15,000 globular star clusters.
Our Milky Way has only a few hundred billion stars and about 150 globular clusters.
A jet of tiny particles, powered by a black hole, streams out of its centre at nearly the speed of light.

The galaxy is so big that Hubble had to take two side-by-side pictures to cover all of its spiral arms.
